newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In Knock, knock, knocking on Net Nirvana's door.
newsitem.headline: Plugged In Knock, knock, knocking on Net Nirvana's door.

text.p: Video on demand is one of those concepts that many have talked about but few have delivered.

We have heard much about how one day companies will deliver video on demand through that thing called interactive television. Those services have been slow in coming and more than a few have been tiring of hearing about trials underway in such places as Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan that will lead to commercial services around the turn of this or that century.

But the arrival of the Net has been circumventing all this by offering a low-cost communications alternative without the heavy infrastructure buildup. And the Net is increasingly what you want it to be: an information highway, a news source, an entertainment source or even an industrial pipeline.

The folks over at Progressive Networks, the same people who brought us RealAudio two years ago, believe it is their mission to help make the Internet into this new mass medium that many have been pushing for. As part of this mission, they released in time for Valentine's Day last week a new Internet toy called the RealPlayer.

You can download a free version of the player at their site (http://www.real.com). It takes the hard drive a few minutes to embrace it but the installation process once you are finished is relatively easy. It also attaches itself to your Web browsers and runs quickly once called upon to display a video on the Internet.
RealPlayer and other such devices hold much promise for the digital world because it will allow surfers to pick and choose what films, newscasts or specials they want to see when they to view them.

"The introduction of high-quality audio and video over the Internet and Intranets enables entertainment, publishing, broadcast companies and corporations to deliver highly compelling images and sounds to audiences over personal computers and web devices," said Jae Kim, research analyst at Paul Kagan Associates, Carmel, Calif.
More than 60 companies have climbed aboard the RealPlayer bandwagon, including such heavyweights as ABC Online, AT&T, and the BBC.

"C-SPAN announced that it will use RealVideo to broadcast more than 10 hours of live programming per day, 7-days-per-week on the web. The Fox News Channel also said it would use RealVideo to broadcast its cable news channel 24-hours-per-day for a two-week period, then selective programming later.
ABC announced plans to cover the eight-weeks of Hollywood's Oscar hoopla, leading up to the March awards ceremony," gushed the company's press release.

From the RealPlayer site, you could zoom to several sites to test out the video player, including viewing the three videos premiered for the RealPlayer by Hollywood producer Spike Lee (http://www.timecast.com/spikelee/theater/lobby.html).

"With the quality of RealVideo, artists and filmmakers can now show their work to millions worldwide using the Internet," said Lee in a statement. "The Internet clearly has become an emerging new medium and the addition of quality video takes it one step closer to becoming a true mass medium."

One of Lee's videos was an interview with actor John Turturro, who played the memorable loser in the movie Quiz Show. The video size was small and the display choppy but it was an engaging few minutes on the Net. You also had to put up with an Orwellian type phrase, "Net congestion, rebuffing" that kept popping up and halting the flow of the mini-programme.

Nevertheless, even with the shortcomings, there was a feeling that we are perhaps months and not years away from some compelling applications for Internet surfers. Slow modems speeds and the congestion of the Internet is general will continues to be major stumbling blocks for many users of video and audio players. But, suddenly, it seems, Net Nirvana is coming into focus.
